questions.stem: Two power-driven vessels are crossing with risk of collision. Which one keeps out of the way?
options: The vessel which has the other on her own port side
The one with the other on her starboard side
The faster of the two vessels
The vessel that sights the other first
questions.explanation: Rule 15(a) gives the duty to the vessel that has the other on her own starboard side. The vessel with the other on her port side is the stand-on vessel. Speed and who sighted whom first are not part of the rule.

questions.stem: In a crossing situation, what does Rule 15 say the give-way vessel should avoid, if the circumstances of the case admit?
options: Slowing down or stopping
Altering course to starboard
Crossing ahead of the other vessel
Sounding any whistle signal
questions.explanation: The give-way vessel should, if the circumstances admit, avoid crossing ahead of the stand-on vessel. Slowing down and altering to starboard to pass astern are the usual correct actions, and nothing in Rule 15 forbids sound signals (Rule 34 covers them).

questions.stem: At night, in a power-driven vessel, you see a white masthead light and a red sidelight on your starboard bow. The bearing is steady and the range is closing. What is your role?
options: Stand-on vessel; keep your course and speed
Give-way; act early and substantially
Head-on; both to starboard
Overtaking vessel; keep clear until past
questions.explanation: Seeing her red sidelight means you are on her port side, so she has you on her port side and you have her on your starboard side. You are the give-way vessel. Head-on would show both sidelights, and an overtaking approach would show only a sternlight.

questions.stem: You are the give-way vessel in a crossing situation with plenty of sea room. Which action best fits Rules 15 and 16?
options: Increase speed to cross ahead of her quickly
An early, bold turn to starboard to pass astern
Alter 5 degrees to port and watch the bearing
Keep your course and speed and sound five short blasts
questions.explanation: An early, substantial turn to starboard to pass astern keeps you clear and avoids crossing ahead. Speeding up to cross ahead is what Rule 15 tells you to avoid. A small port turn is neither substantial nor sensible. Holding course is the stand-on vessel's role.

questions.stem: Rule 15 decides who gives way when which two vessels cross?
options: Any two vessels
Two power-driven vessels
A power-driven vessel and a sailing vessel
Two sailing vessels
questions.explanation: Rule 15(a) is written for two power-driven vessels. Two sailing vessels use Rule 12, and a power-driven vessel and a sailing vessel use Rule 18 (unless one is overtaking).

questions.stem: You are crossing a river in Canadian waters (not the St. Lawrence). A power-driven vessel is coming down the river on your port side, bearing steady. Under the Canadian Rule 15(b), which is correct?
options: She has you on her starboard side, so she must keep out of the way
You keep clear: you cross, she descends
Both alter to starboard
The vessel going against the current is always the give-way vessel
questions.explanation: Rule 15(b) applies notwithstanding paragraph (a): in Canadian waters a vessel crossing a river keeps out of the way of a power-driven vessel ascending or descending it. The usual starboard-side test would make her give way, which is the trap. The 'against the current' idea comes from the Canadian Rule 9 narrow-channel paragraph, which is about vessels meeting, not crossing.

questions.stem: Where does the Canadian river-crossing paragraph, Rule 15(b), NOT apply?
options: On the Fraser River in BC
On the St. Lawrence seaward of Ile Rouge
On any river in the Great Lakes Basin
On rivers narrower than 500 metres
questions.explanation: Rule 15(b) applies in Canadian waters except on the St. Lawrence River seaward of Ile Rouge. There is no width limit in the rule, and nothing excludes the Fraser or the Great Lakes Basin rivers.
